prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of GLP-1 and its active form that made possible incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: After the full exchange I still rank B014 first and as a single-achievement prize, and the reason is the science, not the six-for-six opening. The chain from proglucagon processing and the insulinotropic action of GLP-1 to the identification of the active GLP-1(7-36) form, and then to long-acting agonists, is unusually complete. It has been confirmed by large independent randomized trials in glycaemia, weight, cardiovascular and renal outcomes, and the interpretation has been stable for decades, so maturity is not in doubt. Holst and Drucker are the core on which all six of us agree. For the third seat I answer the chair's first question this way: the citation should be anchored on the physiology of the hormone and its active form, with the therapies named as the consequence and not as the credited achievement. Under that anchor the third laureate is Mojsov. The identification and synthesis of the active peptide is a discovery step in the physiology that has no substitute, whereas the long-acting analogues are optimisation of a concept already established. A single part also avoids the four-name problem that a B014 plus B003 pairing would create under the three-person limit.
statement.case_against: The weakness is still credit. My trio excludes Knudsen, whose work turned a peptide with a half-life of minutes into a weekly drug, and that is why patients benefit at all. Habener's group is also outside the credited names. If the committee decides that the achievement is physiology plus therapy, my trio is harder to defend and the Drucker, Holst and Knudsen trio becomes the more coherent one. The Mojsov position also depends on the priority record for the active peptide, which is contested and which I hold partly from memory. I cannot document it from the supplied materials, and a citation resting on a first-identification claim would be fragile. A prize that leaves out the industrial developer may also be read as ignoring why the discovery mattered clinically.

responses.point: The chair argues that identification of GLP-1(7-36) clarified the biology but the clinical impact followed from long-acting agonists, so the translational step should hold the third seat, and he asks that his reliance on memory of the priority history be recorded.
responses.response: I accept the caveat and apply it to myself, since my reading of the priority history is also partly from memory. I agree that the clinical impact came from the long-acting agonists, but I do not think that makes it the discovery to credit. The prize is for physiology or medicine, and the impact of the analogues rests on the physiology Holst and Drucker established and on the identification of the active form. I have not moved on this. You and I disagree about weight, not about facts, and I would not call either trio indefensible. In answer to your own question about whether the split can be bridged, the citation I propose names the therapies as a consequence, which gives you the translational end in the wording without placing a person on it.

responses.point: El-Manira asks the committee to state explicitly whether the prize honours physiology plus therapy or physiology alone, because that choice settles the third name, and he says he would change his view if priority for the active peptide is clearly documented.
responses.response: I agree that this is the decision and that the science is not in dispute. My answer is physiology alone as the credited achievement, with therapy as its demonstrated consequence. Your condition cuts both ways. The record supplied to us does not document priority for the active peptide well enough to settle it, so I do not claim Mojsov's claim is proven, only that identification and synthesis of the active form is a discovery step. If the committee instead votes that therapy must be credited explicitly, I would move to your trio and not block it. I take your point that Knudsen's step was creative science and not mere engineering, and I have softened the word industrial in my own thinking.

responses.point: Linnarsson says the Nobel criteria concern the discovery and its consequences, not the employer, and that long-acting analogues were not an obvious consequence of the physiology because of the peptide half-life problem.
responses.response: This is a fair correction of how I framed Knudsen in round 1. Employer is not a reason to exclude, and I withdraw any suggestion that it is. The half-life problem was real and its solution was not obvious. My reason for preferring Mojsov is therefore not that industry work is lesser. It is that the committee has to name three people, and the physiology is the achievement that the later drugs depend on. I accept that Nobel history includes translational steps when they are inseparable from the discovery. I put a high bar on that here because the active peptide and the analogue both sit on the same chain and one seat cannot cover both.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius proposes wording the citation around the physiology and the active form of GLP-1 and not around a single first-identification claim, because Habener is outside the credited list, and says Knudsen is where the real trade-off lies.
responses.response: I agree and have adopted that wording. My citation says physiology of GLP-1 and its active form, which avoids a statement about who was first. It is also the answer to the chair's question on the Habener group. I do not think that group's early work changes the allocation among the four credited names, but I cannot verify that, and the citation should not claim more than the record supports. I also agree that if the committee wants a translational flavour, the trade-off is between Mojsov and Knudsen and not Drucker.

responses.point: Perlmann reminds us that the primary priority literature should be checked before the final ballot, and that B039 carries the unresolved Eshhar question and open issues of toxicity and solid tumours, so it is not an automatic fallback.
responses.response: I agree on both. We cannot verify priority within this process, and a final ballot should be read with that limit in mind. On B039, I take your point and I have moved on one detail from round 1: I would now drop Rosenberg and keep June and Sadelain, because the chair and Linnarsson are right that the engineered-receptor discovery is distinct from adoptive cell transfer. Eshhar's absence from the credited names remains a real obstacle, so I keep B039 as the first alternative only because its clinical consequence is documented in approved products, and B003 as the cleaner credit but with less mature medical impact.

uncertainties: Whether the third seat should go to Mojsov or Knudsen. This depends on whether the committee credits physiology alone or physiology plus therapy, and the priority literature on the active peptide cannot be verified from the supplied materials.

Whether the early proglucagon and GLP-1 work of the Habener group, which is outside the credited names, should change the allocation. I think it can be handled in the citation wording but I cannot confirm this.

Whether B039 would be workable at all with June and Sadelain given Eshhar's absence, and whether B003 could be framed as a second part without exceeding three people, which it could not alongside a three-person B014.
Long-term durability and safety of incretin therapy in obesity are still accumulating, though I do not treat this as a maturity barrier.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for the shortlisted candidates, and the round 1 exchange has not changed that. I have co-authored with colleagues in KI single-cell genomics, including Linnarsson and Frisen, but none of that work concerns the shortlisted discoveries or any credited person, and I infer no tie from shared institutions or topics.
